Vitamin C

Vitamin C
Other namesAscorbic acid
FormulaC6H8O6
Molar mass176.12 g/mol
CAS Number50-81-7

Vitamin C, also known as ascorbic acid, is a water-soluble vitamin found in citrus and other fruits and vegetables. It is an essential nutrient for people, who need it to repair tissue and to make collagen. A lack of it causes scurvy, whose early signs are tiredness, sore gums and easy bruising.[1]

Biology

Most animals make their own vitamin C in the liver or the kidneys. People, the other apes, guinea pigs and many bats cannot, because the gene for the last enzyme of the pathway no longer works. The body keeps only a small store of the vitamin, so it has to be eaten often.

Deficiency

Scurvy appears after one to three months with little or no vitamin C. Bleeding gums, poor wound healing and joint pain follow, and scurvy that is not treated can kill. It is rare today but still seen in people who eat very few fruits and vegetables.

Sources

Fruits and vegetables supply nearly all the vitamin C in most diets, though the amounts vary with the kind, the season and the storage.

Plant sources

Rose hips, guavas, blackcurrants, kiwifruit, sweet peppers and broccoli hold more vitamin C per gram than oranges. Citrus fruits such as oranges, lemons and grapefruit are a good everyday source. Potatoes supply much of the vitamin C eaten in some northern countries in winter.

Animal sources

Fresh liver holds more vitamin C than muscle meat, and raw fish roe and some seal and whale tissues were the winter source for Arctic peoples. Cow's milk is a poor source, and much of what it has is lost when the milk is heated.

Food preparation

Vitamin C breaks down in heat and dissolves in cooking water, so boiling vegetables for a long time loses much of it. Steaming, or eating the fruit raw, keeps more of it.

History

In 1747 the naval surgeon James Lind showed in a trial at sea that citrus fruit cured scurvy among sailors. The vitamin was isolated in the 1920s and 1930s, and Albert Szent-Gyorgyi received a Nobel Prize in 1937 for his part in the work.

pages.wikipedia/Vitamin_B12:
Vitamin B12

Vitamin B12, also called cobalamin, is a water-soluble vitamin that the body needs to make red blood cells and to keep the nerves working. A lack of it causes a kind of anaemia and nerve damage that may not get better.

Deficiency

Deficiency is most common in older people, in people with stomach or bowel disease, and in people who eat no animal foods. Signs include tiredness, pale skin, a sore tongue, and numbness or tingling in the hands and feet.

Sources

Bacteria and archaea

Only some bacteria and archaea can make vitamin B12; neither plants nor animals can make it themselves. Animals take it in from the bacteria in their gut or in their food.

Animal-derived foods

Meat, liver, shellfish, eggs, milk and fish carry the vitamin B12 that the animals took in. Liver and clams hold the most of any common food.

Plants and algae

Plants are not a reliable source of vitamin B12, so people who eat no animal foods need fortified foods or supplements. Some seaweeds hold forms of the vitamin that the body cannot use.

Fortified foods

Some breakfast cereals, plant milks and nutritional yeast have vitamin B12 added during manufacture.

Medical uses

Vitamin B12 is given by injection or by mouth to treat deficiency. Large doses by mouth work even in many people who absorb it poorly.

pages.wikimed/Foodborne_illness:
Foodborne illness

Foodborne illness, commonly called food poisoning, is any illness caused by eating food contaminated with germs, their toxins or chemicals. It often comes on suddenly and usually lasts a few days.

Signs and symptoms

Symptoms vary with the cause and may begin within hours or take days to appear.

  • Digestive:
    • nausea and vomiting
    • stomach cramps
    • watery or bloody diarrhoea
  • Whole body:
    • fever and chills
    • headache and tiredness
  • Nerves, with some causes such as botulism:
    • blurred or double vision
    • trouble swallowing
    • weakness that spreads down from the face

Causes

Most cases are caused by bacteria, viruses or parasites; a few come from chemicals or natural poisons in food.

  • Bacteria
    • Salmonella, from undercooked eggs and poultry
    • Campylobacter, from raw milk and poultry
    • Listeria, from soft cheese and chilled ready meals
  • Viruses
    • norovirus, the commonest cause
    • hepatitis A
  • Parasites
    • Giardia, from untreated water
    • tapeworms, from undercooked pork or beef

Prevention

Washing hands, cooking meat right through, keeping cold food cold and hot food hot, and keeping raw meat away from food that will not be cooked all lower the risk. Leftovers should be cooled quickly and eaten within a few days.

Treatment

Most people get better on their own within a few days. The main danger is dehydration, which is treated by drinking oral rehydration solution. Seek medical care for bloody diarrhoea, a high fever, signs of dehydration, or symptoms in a baby, an older person or a pregnant woman.

Epidemiology

Foodborne illness is common: the World Health Organization estimates that about one person in ten in the world falls ill from contaminated food each year. Children under five carry a large share of the burden.

pages.wikipedia/Vaccine:
Vaccine

A vaccine is a biological preparation that gives active acquired immunity to a particular infectious disease. A vaccine typically contains an agent that looks like a disease-causing germ and is often made from weakened or killed forms of the germ, its toxins, or one of its surface proteins. The agent trains the immune system to recognise the germ and destroy it later.

Effectiveness

Vaccines have ended smallpox and nearly ended polio. Protection is not total: some vaccinated people still catch the disease, usually in a milder form, including measles and whooping cough. How well a vaccine works depends on the person's age, health and genes.

Types

  • Inactivated vaccines are made from germs that have been killed with heat or chemicals.
    • polio (injected)
    • rabies
    • hepatitis A
  • Live attenuated vaccines hold living germs that have been weakened so they cannot cause disease in healthy people.
    • measles, mumps and rubella
    • yellow fever
    • oral polio
  • Toxoid vaccines are made from toxins made harmless.
    • tetanus
    • diphtheria
  • Messenger RNA vaccines carry instructions that let the body's own cells make one protein of the virus for a short time.

Excipients

Besides the active part, a vaccine may hold other substances, each in very small amounts:

  • Aluminium salts or gels, added as adjuvants to give a stronger immune response.
  • Preservatives such as thiomersal, used in some multi-dose vials to stop contamination.
  • Stabilisers such as sugars or gelatin, which keep the vaccine working during storage.
  • Traces of egg protein in vaccines grown in hens' eggs, such as most flu vaccines.

History

Edward Jenner showed in 1796 that matter from cowpox sores protected people against smallpox. Louis Pasteur made the first vaccines weakened in a laboratory, for chicken cholera and for rabies, in the 1880s.

Society and culture

Many countries include vaccines in free childhood programmes, including those against measles, polio and tetanus. Opposition to vaccines, including false claims that link them to autism, has led to outbreaks of measles. Some countries require proof of vaccination for school entry, including the United States and France.

pages.wikipedia/Cell_(biology):
Cell (biology)

The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of all forms of life. Every cell comes from the division of another cell. The study of cells is called cell biology.

Cell types

Cells are of two types: prokaryotic cells, which have no nucleus, and eukaryotic cells, which keep their DNA in a nucleus. Prokaryotes include bacteria and archaea. Eukaryotes include animals, plants, fungi and many single-celled organisms. Eukaryotic cells are usually about ten times wider than prokaryotic ones.

Cell components

All cells are enclosed in a membrane that holds a watery cytoplasm, in which the cell's other parts float. The cytoplasm contains many enzymes that speed up the cell's chemistry.

Membrane

The cell membrane is a double layer of lipids with proteins set in it. It lets some substances through and keeps others out. Plant cells and fungi also have a cell wall outside the membrane, which includes cellulose in plants and chitin in fungi.

Genetic material

A cell's genes are carried in DNA. In eukaryotic cells most of the DNA is in the nucleus, and a little is in the mitochondria and, in plants, the chloroplasts. Bacteria often contain small rings of DNA called plasmids, including the ones that carry resistance to antibiotics.

Organelles

Organelles are the parts of a cell that each do one job.

  • Nucleus – holds most of the cell's DNA and controls which genes are used.
  • Mitochondria – make most of the cell's supply of energy, as ATP.
  • Ribosomes – build proteins from the instructions carried by RNA.
  • Chloroplasts – found in plants and algae, capture light to make sugar.

Chemistry

By weight a typical cell is about 70 percent water. Most of the rest is protein, with smaller parts of lipids, nucleic acids and carbohydrates. A human body is thought to be made of about 37 trillion cells.

History

Robert Hooke named cells in 1665 after the small rooms of a monastery, when he saw them in cork through a microscope. The cell theory, that all living things are made of cells, was set out by Schleiden and Schwann in 1838 and 1839.

Mount Everest

Mount Everest
Elevation8,848.86 m (29,031.7 ft)
LocationNepal and China (Tibet)
Parent rangeHimalayas

Coordinates27°59′N 86°55′E

Mount Everest is Earth's highest mountain above sea level, in the Mahalangur Himal range of the Himalayas. The border between China and Nepal runs across its summit.

Name

The Tibetan name is Chomolungma and the Nepali name is Sagarmatha. The English name honours George Everest, a surveyor general of India, and was given in 1865.

Geology

The upper mountain is made of layers of limestone, shale and marble that were once the floor of an ocean; fossils of sea creatures are found near the summit. The mountain still rises by a few millimetres a year as India pushes into Asia.

Climbing

Routes

The two main routes are the southeast ridge from Nepal and the north ridge from Tibet. Most climbers reach the Nepal base camp on foot from the airstrip at Lukla, a trek of about a week. Climbers use bottled oxygen above about 8,000 metres.

Dangers

Climbers face altitude sickness, avalanches, falls and extreme cold, and more than 300 people have died on the mountain. Most deaths happen above 8,000 metres, in the area called the death zone.

Tourism

Tens of thousands of trekkers visit the Everest region each year, and the money they spend supports many families. Waste left on the mountain has become a problem, and climbers must now carry their rubbish down.

pages.wikipedia/Solder:
Solder

Solder is a metal alloy with a low melting point, used to join metal parts and to make electrical connections. It is melted with a soldering iron or a flame and flows into the joint, where it sets.

Lead-based solders

For most of the twentieth century the usual electronics solder was 63 parts tin to 37 parts lead, which melts at 183 °C. Plumbing solder once held as much as half lead, which is why many countries, including the United States, banned it for drinking water pipes in the 1980s. Lead solders are still allowed in some uses, including aircraft and military electronics.

Lead-free solders

European rules of 2006 pushed most consumer electronics to lead-free solder. Lead-free solders are mostly tin with a few percent of silver and a little copper, a mix known as SAC. They melt about 30 °C higher than tin-lead solder, so they need a hotter iron and give duller joints.

Flux

Electronics solder contains a core of flux, a substance that cleans the metal so the solder can wet it. Common fluxes include rosin, made from pine resin, and water-soluble organic acids. Acid flux used for plumbing must never be used on electronics, because what is left behind eats the copper. Some fluxes leave a residue that includes salts, which must be washed off.

Safety

The smoke from heated flux irritates the eyes and lungs, so solder where the air moves. Wash your hands after handling lead solder, and keep it away from food and children. Hot solder can spit, so eye protection is advised, including for people watching.

Other uses

Jewellers use hard solders that include silver and melt at much higher temperatures. Stained glass makers join their pieces with tin-lead solder over copper foil or lead strips.

pages.wikipedia/Atmosphere_of_Earth:
Atmosphere of Earth

The atmosphere of Earth is the layer of gases, known as air, held around the planet by gravity. It protects life by absorbing ultraviolet light from the Sun and by evening out the temperature between day and night.

Composition

By volume, dry air is about 78 percent nitrogen, 21 percent oxygen and nearly 1 percent argon. Carbon dioxide makes up about 0.04 percent. Air also contains a varying amount of water vapour, on average about 1 percent at sea level.

Layers

The atmosphere is divided into layers by how the temperature changes with height, including the troposphere, the stratosphere, the mesosphere and the thermosphere. The troposphere contains about three quarters of the mass of the atmosphere and nearly all its water vapour. The stratosphere includes the ozone layer, which absorbs most ultraviolet light.

Pressure

Air pressure at sea level is about 101 kilopascals and halves roughly every 5.5 kilometres of height. Weather maps include lines of equal pressure, called isobars. Low pressure usually brings clouds and rain, including most storms.

Evolution

Earth's first atmosphere was mostly hydrogen and helium and was soon lost to space. Oxygen built up about 2.4 billion years ago, after bacteria in shallow seas began to release it. The change, known as the Great Oxidation Event, killed many organisms, including most that could not live with oxygen.

Climate

Greenhouse gases, including carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour, keep the surface about 33 °C warmer than it would be without them. Burning fossil fuels has raised the amount of carbon dioxide by about half since 1750. Human activities also release pollutants, including soot and sulfur dioxide, that harm health.

pages.wikipedia/Sun:
Sun

The Sun is the star at the centre of the Solar System. It is a nearly perfect ball of hot plasma, heated by nuclear fusion in its core, and it is by far the most important source of energy for life on Earth.

General characteristics

The Sun is about 109 times as wide as Earth and about 330,000 times as heavy. It contains about 99.86 percent of the mass of the Solar System. Its family includes eight planets, including Earth, and many smaller bodies.

Composition

The Sun is mostly hydrogen, about three quarters of its mass, with helium making up nearly all the rest. Heavier elements such as oxygen, carbon, neon and iron make up less than 2 percent.

Structure

The Sun's interior includes the core, the radiative zone and the convective zone. The core contains about a third of the Sun's mass in a fortieth of its volume. The visible surface, the photosphere, has a temperature of about 5,800 kelvins.

Activity

The Sun's magnetic field causes sunspots, flares and coronal mass ejections, including the storms that make the northern lights. Its activity rises and falls over a cycle of about eleven years.

Life cycle

The Sun formed about 4.6 billion years ago from a cloud of gas and dust that included material from earlier stars. In about five billion years it will swell into a red giant.

pages.wikimed/Blood:
Blood

Blood is a body fluid that carries oxygen and nutrients to the cells and takes their waste away. In people it is pumped round the body by the heart through the arteries and veins.

Functions

Blood carries oxygen from the lungs and carbon dioxide back to them. It also carries hormones and heat, and its white cells and antibodies fight infection, including infections of the skin and lungs. Clotting stops bleeding from small wounds.

Constituents

Blood is about 55 percent plasma and 45 percent cells by volume. Plasma is mostly water, with dissolved proteins, sugar, salts, hormones and carbon dioxide. The cells are red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets.

Red blood cells

Red blood cells contain haemoglobin, an iron-rich protein that binds oxygen and gives blood its colour. Each lives about 120 days. A drop of blood includes millions of them.

White blood cells

White blood cells defend the body; they include lymphocytes, which make antibodies, and neutrophils, which eat bacteria.

Volume

An adult has about 5 litres of blood, roughly 7 percent of body weight. Losing more than a third of it quickly is life-threatening.

Blood types

Blood types include the ABO groups and the Rhesus factor. A transfusion must be of a type the patient can receive, including in emergencies, when O negative blood is often used.

pages.wikipedia/Solar_water_disinfection:
Solar water disinfection

Solar water disinfection (SODIS) is a way to make water safer to drink by leaving it in clear plastic bottles in full sunlight. Ultraviolet light and heat from the sun together kill or weaken most germs that cause diarrhoea.

Method

The method needs only clear bottles and sunshine, and it costs almost nothing.

Step 1

Choose clear, unscratched bottles made of PET plastic, no larger than two litres. Glass bottles block much of the ultraviolet light and should not be used.

Remove the labels so that sunlight can reach the water from every side, and wash the bottles before the first use.

Step 2

Fill the bottles with water that is as clear as possible. If the water is cloudy, let it settle or filter it through a folded cloth first, because cloudiness shields germs from the sun.

A simple test: if you can read large print through the bottle from the side, the water is clear enough. Shake the bottle for twenty seconds before filling it to the top, which adds air to the water.

Step 3

Lay the bottles flat in full sun for at least six hours on a sunny day, or for two full days if the sky is more than half cloudy.

Placing the bottles on a sheet of corrugated metal roofing helps them heat up. Make sure they are not shaded by trees or buildings at any time of the day.

  • Do not use the method on days of continuous rain; collect rainwater or boil the water instead.

Step 4

Drink the water straight from the bottle, or pour it into a clean cup. Once opened, the water should be drunk the same day.

Limitations

SODIS does not remove chemicals such as arsenic, fluoride or pesticides from water. It does not work well with water that is very cloudy, and it needs sunshine, so it is less useful in long rainy seasons.

Effectiveness

Studies have found fewer cases of diarrhoea among children in households that use SODIS regularly. The method is promoted by health agencies in many countries of Africa, Asia and Latin America.

pages.wikipedia/First_aid:
First aid

First aid is the first help given to a person with an illness or injury, until full medical treatment is available. Some first aid can be done by anyone with little or no equipment.

Aims

The aims of first aid are often summed up as the three Ps:

  • Preserve life: the first aim of all medical care, including first aid, is to save lives.
  • Prevent further harm: move away from danger, and keep the person still if a spine injury is possible.
  • Promote recovery: start the healing, for example by covering a wound.

Key skills

Many first aid courses teach the steps known by the letters ABC:

  1. Airway
    • Tilt the head back and lift the chin to open the airway.
    • Clear anything blocking the mouth.
  2. Breathing
    • Look, listen and feel for normal breathing for no more than ten seconds.
  3. Circulation
    • If the person is not breathing normally, start chest compressions.
    • Press hard and fast.

Conditions

Bleeding

Press firmly on the wound with a clean cloth and keep pressing; raise the injured part if you can. Do not remove a cloth that has soaked through: put another on top.

Burns

Cool a burn under cool running water for at least twenty minutes, and do not use ice, butter or creams. Cover it loosely with cling film or a clean plastic bag.

Choking

  • Encourage the person to cough.
    • If that fails, give up to five back blows between the shoulder blades.
    • Then give up to five abdominal thrusts.
  • Call for emergency help if the blockage does not clear.

First aid kits

A basic first aid kit typically contains:

  • adhesive bandages of several sizes
  • sterile gauze pads
  • a roll of adhesive tape
  • disposable gloves
  • scissors and tweezers

Cereal

A cereal is a grass grown for the edible parts of its grain. Cereals give more food energy worldwide than any other type of crop.

Major cereals

    • durum wheat, the hard wheat used for pasta
  • Sorghum and millet stand heat and drought, and feed many people in the dry parts of Africa and India.

Whole grains supply starch, protein, fibre, B vitamins and minerals; refining removes most of the fibre and many of the vitamins. Cereal protein is low in lysine, so cereals are best eaten with beans or other pulses.

Production

In 2020 the world grew about 3 billion tonnes of cereals; maize, rice and wheat made up most of it. China, the United States and India grow the most.

Nairobi

Nairobi is the capital and largest city of Kenya. It stands on the Nairobi River in the south of the country, at an altitude of about 1,795 metres.

History

Nairobi was founded in 1899 as a supply depot of the Uganda Railway, and the first trains arrived that year. It became the capital of British East Africa in 1907 and of independent Kenya in 1963.

Geography

Climate

Because of its altitude Nairobi has a mild climate, with a cool season from June to August and two rainy seasons, in March to May and in October to December.

Economy

Nairobi is a centre of business and finance for East Africa, and many international organisations, including a United Nations office, have their headquarters there.

Transport

Air

Jomo Kenyatta International Airport, 15 kilometres south-east of the centre, is the busiest airport in East Africa. Wilson Airport serves small planes and domestic flights.

Rail

The Nairobi Commuter Rail links the centre with the suburbs, and the Madaraka Express runs to Mombasa on the coast in about five hours.

Road

Matatus, privately owned minibuses, are the most common form of public transport in the city. Traffic jams are severe at rush hour, and a bus rapid transit system has been planned for years.

Culture

Cuisine

Nyama choma, grilled meat, is a favourite of the city's restaurants and bars; ugali, a stiff maize porridge, is the everyday staple. Indian food is also common, a legacy of the railway workers who settled in the city.

Crime

Nairobi has a high rate of street crime, and pickpocketing and phone snatching are common in the centre. The city's nickname 'Nairobbery' reflects this reputation.

Moon

The Moon is Earth's only natural satellite. It is about a quarter as wide as Earth, which makes it the largest moon in the Solar System compared with its planet.

Orbit

The Moon takes about 27.3 days to go once around Earth measured against the stars, and about 29.5 days from one new moon to the next. It always shows the same face to Earth because it turns once on its axis in each orbit.

The dark areas, called maria, are plains of old lava; the bright highlands are older and covered in craters. The surface is covered in a fine dust called regolith.

The Soviet Luna 2 was the first craft to reach the Moon, in 1959. Twelve astronauts walked on it between 1969 and 1972.

pages.wikipedia/Mayflower:
Mayflower

The Mayflower was an English ship that carried a group of English families, later called the Pilgrims, to North America in 1620. The voyage has become a founding story of the United States.

Voyage

The ship left Plymouth, England, on 16 September 1620 with 102 passengers and a crew of about thirty. Storms cracked one of its main beams, which the passengers helped to brace with a large iron screw.

Arrival

After 66 days at sea the ship sighted Cape Cod on 9 November and anchored off what is now Provincetown on 11 November 1620. The men signed the Mayflower Compact before going ashore. In December the settlers chose a site and named it Plymouth.

First winter

About half of the passengers and crew died in the first winter, of disease and cold. In the spring, the Wampanoag leader Massasoit made a treaty of peace with the settlers.

Later history

John Carver was chosen as the colony's first governor; after he died in April 1621, William Bradford took his place and led the colony for most of the next thirty years. The ship itself returned to England and was probably broken up around 1624.

pages.wikimed/Diabetes:
Diabetes

Diabetes mellitus is a group of common conditions in which the blood sugar stays high for a long time. Over years it damages the blood vessels, nerves, eyes and kidneys.

Types

  • Type 1 – the pancreas makes too little insulin; it usually begins in childhood.
  • Type 2 – the body responds poorly to insulin; it is linked to weight and inactivity and makes up about 90 percent of cases.
  • Gestational diabetes – high blood sugar in pregnancy in a woman without diabetes before.

Signs and symptoms

The classic symptoms are frequent urination, increased thirst, increased hunger and weight loss without trying. Type 2 diabetes may give no symptoms for years.

Diagnosis

Diabetes is diagnosed with one of these blood tests:

  • fasting blood sugar of 7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL) or higher
  • HbA1c of 48 mmol/mol (6.5 percent) or higher

Management

Diet

A diet with plenty of vegetables, whole grains and pulses and little added sugar helps to control blood sugar. Regular meals help people who take insulin to avoid low blood sugar.

Medications

Type 1 diabetes needs insulin injections for life. Metformin is usually the first medicine tried for type 2.

Complications

Long-term high blood sugar damages blood vessels, which can lead to heart disease, stroke, kidney failure, blindness and foot ulcers.

pages.wikimed/Snakebite:
Snakebite

A snakebite is an injury caused by the bite of a snake, especially a venomous one. Many bites by venomous snakes inject little or no venom.

Signs and symptoms

Common signs of a venomous bite are pain, swelling and bruising at the bite, followed by vomiting, blurred vision, tingling, sweating, bleeding or weakness, depending on the snake.

Prevention

Wearing boots and long trousers, using a torch at night, and not putting hands into holes or under rocks lower the risk of being bitten.

Treatment

First aid

Keep the person calm and still, remove rings and tight clothing near the bite, and carry them to medical care as fast as possible. Do not cut the wound, suck out the venom, or apply ice. For bites by some snakes, wrapping the whole limb firmly with a bandage and keeping it still is advised.

Antivenom

Antivenom is the main treatment for serious envenomation, and it works best when given early. It must be given in a hospital, because allergic reactions are common.

Epidemiology

Snakebites kill between 80,000 and 140,000 people a year, most of them in rural Africa and Asia.

pages.wikivoyage/Lakeport:
Lakeport

Lakeport is a town of about 90,000 people on the eastern shore of Lake Mwezi, and the main base for trips to the islands and the hill forests.

Understand

Lakeport grew up around a fishing harbour; the first settlers arrived from the coast in the 1880s, when traders set up a market by the shore. The railway reached the town in 1931 and made it the main port of the lake.

The town is hot and humid from February to April, and the long rains fall from April to June. The tourist office on Harbour Road has maps and lists of boat operators.

Get in

By plane

Lakeport Airport (LKP) has two flights a day from the capital; international travellers arrive first at the capital's airport and change there.

The airport is 8 km north of town. A shuttle bus meets every flight and runs to the bus station, and a taxi costs about 800 shillings.

By bus

Overnight coaches from the capital take ten hours and arrive at the main bus station on Market Road. Day buses are cheaper but slower and stop in every village.

By boat

A ferry from the islands arrives at the old harbour three times a week, weather permitting.

Get around

The centre is small enough to walk, though the heat makes it tiring in the afternoon.

By minibus

Shared minibuses run from the bus station along the shore road; tell the driver where you want to stop and pay when you get off.

By motorbike taxi

Motorbike taxis wait on most corners. They are quick and cheap, but insist on a helmet and agree on the fare before you get on.

By bicycle

Bicycles can be hired by the day at the harbour; the shore road is flat and has little traffic.

See

  • Lake Museum, Harbour Road. Daily 9AM–5PM. Old fishing boats, nets and photographs of the town's early days. 300 shillings.
  • Old Market, The covered market from the 1920s, busiest on Saturday mornings, with fish, spices and cloth.
  • Bird Island, Pelicans and cormorants nest on this rocky island; boats leave from the harbour in the morning.

Do

  • Boat trips, to the islands leave the harbour every morning; a half day costs about 2,000 shillings per boat.
  • Hill forest walk, A marked trail climbs through the forest to a viewpoint over the lake; allow four hours and take water.
  • Fishing, with local fishermen at dawn can be arranged at the harbour; bring a hat and expect to help with the nets.
  • Cooking class, Learn to cook fish curry and chapati in a family kitchen near the market; book a day ahead.

Buy

Most shops and restaurants take only cash; there are three ATMs on Market Road, and the larger hotels accept cards. Bargaining is normal in the market but not in shops with marked prices.

Eat

Fried tilapia with ugali is the local favourite, served at small places all along the shore.

Budget

  • Mama Rose's, Shore Road. Fried fish, beans and chapati at plastic tables by the water. Mains 300 shillings.
  • Station Café, by the bus station. Tea, samosas and rice dishes from early morning until late.
  • Night stalls, Market Square. Grilled maize, skewers of goat meat and fresh juice after dark.

Mid-range

  • Lakeview Restaurant, Harbour Road. Curries and grilled fish on a terrace over the water. Mains 900 shillings.
  • Green Garden, Vegetarian dishes, salads and fruit juices in a quiet garden behind the church.

Splurge

  • The Jetty, The town's best fish dinner, with a view of the sunset over the lake; booking advised at weekends.

Drink

Most bars are along Shore Road and stay open until late at weekends.

  • Fisherman's Bar, Cold beer and live music on Friday and Saturday nights.
  • Sunset Lounge, Cocktails and fruit juices on a rooftop over the harbour.

Sleep

Budget

  • Harbour Guest House, Simple rooms with fans and shared bathrooms, 1,500 shillings a night.

Mid-range

  • Lake Hotel, Rooms with air conditioning, a pool and a restaurant, 6,000 shillings a night.

Stay safe

Lakeport is generally safe, but walk with others or take a taxi after dark, and keep phones out of sight in the market, where bag snatching happens.

If something is stolen, report it at the central police station on Market Road and ask for a written report for your insurance.

Do not swim in the lake at dusk: hippos come close to the shore in the evening.

Stay healthy

Lakeport is in a malaria area: sleep under a net and use repellent in the evening.

Drink bottled or boiled water; the tap water is not safe to drink.

Street food that is cooked hot in front of you is usually safe, but avoid salads and cut fruit that may have been washed in tap water.

The District Hospital on Hospital Road has a 24-hour emergency department, and there are several pharmacies on Market Road.

Connect

Mobile coverage is good in town; SIM cards are sold at the bus station on showing a passport.

Go next

  • The capital, overnight coaches leave the bus station at 8PM every evening and arrive at dawn.
  • Hill Town, two hours by minibus, cooler and greener, with tea estates.
  • The islands, by ferry three times a week from the old harbour.
pages.wikivoyage/Tamaro:
Tamaro

Tamaro is a country in East Africa, with a coast on the Indian Ocean, high plateaus in the west and some of the largest wildlife reserves on the continent.

Regions

  • Coast, beaches, old stone towns and coral reefs
  • Central Highlands, tea country, cool weather and the capital
  • Western Plateau, lakes, forests and the great national parks

Cities

  • Port Amani, the capital and largest city, a busy port
  • Lakeport, on the shore of Lake Mwezi
  • Kilele, a hill town and trekking base

Understand

History

The coast traded with Arabia and India for a thousand years before European ships arrived in the 1500s. Tamaro became independent in 1961 and has held multi-party elections since 1992.

Climate

The best time to visit is the dry season from June to October, when wildlife gathers at the rivers. The coast is hot all year, and the highlands are cool at night.

Talk

Swahili and English are the official languages; English is widely spoken in towns and in the tourist trade, and a few words of Swahili are much appreciated.

Get in

Entry requirements

Most visitors need an e-visa, which must be applied for online at least a week before travel; citizens of neighbouring countries need only a passport. Passports must be valid for six months after arrival.

By plane

Amani International Airport near Port Amani has flights from Europe, the Gulf and across Africa. Kilele also has an international airport with flights from Europe in the high season.

By land

There are border crossings with all the neighbouring countries; the busiest is on the highway north of Lakeport, open from 6AM to 10PM.

Get around

By train

A modern railway runs from Port Amani to the Central Highlands in five hours, with two trains a day; book a day ahead.

By bus

Long-distance buses link all the towns and are cheap, but drivers can be reckless; choose a company with a good name.

By car

Driving is on the left. Roads between the main towns are paved, but many park roads need a four-wheel drive.

See

The great national parks of the Western Plateau are the main attraction, with lions, elephants and the yearly migration of wildebeest. The old stone towns of the coast are a World Heritage Site.

Do

Safaris, diving on the coral reefs, climbing the volcano near Kilele and visiting tea estates are the most popular activities. Hot air balloon flights over the parks can be booked through the lodges.

Buy

The currency is the Tamaro shilling. Credit cards are accepted in large hotels and some restaurants in the capital, but carry cash everywhere else. ATMs are found in all towns.

Eat

The staple is ugali, a stiff porridge of maize flour, eaten with stews of beans, greens or meat. On the coast, fish cooked in coconut milk is the speciality.

Drink

The legal drinking age is 18. Local beer is cheap and good, and tea grown in the highlands is drunk everywhere with milk and sugar.

Sleep

Accommodation ranges from simple guest houses in the towns to luxury tented camps in the parks, which should be booked months ahead for the dry season.

Stay safe

Police roadblocks are common on the highways. If you are stopped, stay calm, show your documents, and ask for a written receipt for any fine.

Crime against visitors is mostly petty theft in the cities; violent crime is rare outside a few districts of the capital.

Stay healthy

A yellow fever vaccination certificate is required if you arrive from a country where the disease is found. Malaria is present below 1,800 metres, so take tablets and sleep under a net.

Respect

Dress modestly away from the beaches, especially on the coast and when visiting a mosque. Always ask before photographing people.
pages.wikivoyage/Kilele:
Kilele

Kilele is a hill town at 3,400 metres in the western mountains of Tamaro, the base for treks to the crater lakes and the volcano.

Understand

At this altitude the nights are cold all year and the sun is strong by day. Many visitors feel the altitude on their first day.

Get in

Kilele airport has daily flights from Port Amani, and buses from the capital take twelve hours over the pass. Arriving by bus lets the body get used to the height more slowly than flying.

Get around

The old town is compact but steep; taxis are cheap and wait at the main square.

See

  • Crater lakes, Three blue lakes in old volcanic craters, an hour by road from town.
  • Cathedral, The stone cathedral on the main square, built in the 1890s.

Do

  • Trekking, Guided treks to the crater lakes take two to four days; agencies on the main square rent tents and stoves.
  • White-water rafting, on the river below town, half a day or full day trips from June to October.
  • Horse riding, Half-day rides through the farms and forests above the town.
  • Volcano climb, A long day climb to the rim of the volcano, 5,100 metres high, best done after a week in town.
  • Hot springs, Soak in the pools of the springs an hour's drive north of town.

Eat

Potato soups, grilled trout from the lakes and roasted maize are the local dishes, served in small family restaurants around the square.

Sleep

  • Square Hostel, Dormitory beds and a kitchen, on the main square.
  • Crater View Hotel, Heated rooms with views over the valley.

Stay healthy

Altitude sickness is common in the first days. Rest on arrival, drink plenty of water and avoid alcohol for the first two days. If the headache, nausea or breathlessness get worse, go down to a lower altitude and see a doctor; do not climb higher with symptoms.

The sun is strong at this height; wear a hat and sunscreen even on cloudy days.

Stay safe

The town is safe, but treks should be made with a registered guide, and the volcano path is dangerous in fog.

Go next

Buses down the valley to the lake towns leave every morning.
pages.wikivoyage/Grassland_National_Park:
Grassland National Park

Grassland National Park is the largest wildlife reserve in Tamaro, a plain of grass and acacia famous for its lions and the yearly migration of wildebeest.

Understand

The park was created in 1951 and covers about 14,000 square kilometres. The migration passes through from July to October.

Get in

The park can be reached by road from Lakeport in three hours; the last 40 km are gravel and need a high vehicle. Small planes fly from Port Amani to three airstrips inside the park.

Fees and permits

Entry costs US$50 per adult per day, paid by card at the gate; children under 16 pay half. Fees are charged for every 24 hours in the park.

Get around

Game drives must be in a closed vehicle, and walking is allowed only with an armed ranger. Roads inside the park are rough tracks, and driving after dark is forbidden.

See

Lions, cheetahs, elephants, giraffes, zebras and huge herds of wildebeest can all be seen, as well as more than 500 kinds of bird.

Do

Game drives at dawn and dusk give the best sightings. Hot air balloon flights at sunrise can be booked at the lodges, and walking safaris with a ranger leave from the main camp.

Sleep

Lodges

Four lodges inside the park have rooms with full board and their own game drives; they are booked months ahead for the migration.

Camping

Public campsites near the river have toilets and cold showers, and must be booked at the gate.

Stay safe

Never leave your vehicle except at marked places. Lions and buffalo are dangerous; at the campsites, do not walk around after dark, and keep food inside the vehicle.
pages.wikivoyage/Port_Amani:
Port Amani

Port Amani is the capital and largest city of Tamaro, a port of about four million people on the Indian Ocean.

Districts

  • Old Town, the historic centre, with the fort and the markets
  • Harbour, the docks, the ferry terminal and the fish market
  • Northern Beaches, hotels and resorts along the sand

Understand

The city's cooking is famous across the region for its coconut curries, grilled seafood and spiced rice, a mix of African, Arab and Indian traditions.

The hottest months are January to March, and the long rains come in April and May.

Get in

By plane

Amani International Airport has flights from Europe, the Gulf and across Africa. Most visitors can get an e-visa online before they arrive; queues at immigration are long in the evening.

By train

Trains from the Central Highlands arrive at Central Station twice a day.

Get around

By train

The airport express train runs from Central Station to the airport every 20 minutes and takes 25 minutes; tickets are sold on the platform.

By taxi

Taxis and ride-hailing cars are everywhere; agree on the fare first or use the app.

See

The Old Town's fort, built by the Portuguese in the 1590s, is the city's best-known sight.

Eat

Port Amani has thousands of places to eat; see the district articles for listings. Many restaurants add a 10% service charge to the bill.

Sleep

Hotels are listed in the district articles; the Northern Beaches have most of the resorts.

Stay safe

Keep valuables out of sight in the Old Town, where pickpockets work the crowds, and take a taxi at night.

Bicycle Chain Replacement

Written By: Robin Wrench
  • Comments: 0

Difficulty

Easy

Steps

2

Time Required

20 minutes

Introduction

A chain stretches as it wears and then wears out the sprockets. This guide shows how to measure the chain and fit a new one.

  • Measure the chain every few hundred kilometres with a chain checker or a ruler.
  • Replace it when twelve links measure more than 12 1/8 inches (308 mm).

Tools

  • Chain Tool

  • Chain Checker

  • Rag

Parts

  • Bicycle Chain

  1. Step 1

    • Shift onto the smallest sprocket at the back and the smallest chainring at the front, so the chain is slack.

    • Place a chain checker on the chain. If it drops fully into the links, the chain is worn and must be replaced. If you do not have a checker, measure twelve full links with a ruler: a new chain measures exactly 12 inches from the first pin to the thirteenth.

    • A chain longer than 12 1/8 inches has stretched too far and will wear the sprockets; at 12 1/4 inches the sprockets usually need replacing as well, because a new chain will skip on them.

    • A chain that skips under load can throw you off the bike. Test the new chain gently before riding in traffic.

    • Clean the chainrings and sprockets with a rag before fitting the new chain, because grit on them shortens the life of the new chain.

    • Count the links of the old chain before you remove it, or lay it beside the new one, so that the new chain can be cut to the same length; most adult bikes need between 108 and 116 links.

    • If the old chain has a master link, it can be opened by squeezing the two plates together with master link pliers.

    • Otherwise push out any pin with the chain tool, turning the handle until the pin is almost out of the outer plate but still held in it.

  2. Step 2

    • Thread the new chain through the rear derailleur, around the smallest sprocket and over the smallest chainring.

    • Join the ends with the master link supplied, or with the joining pin and the chain tool.

    • Lubricate the chain with one drop of chain oil on each roller, and wipe off the excess.

pages.ifixit/Pocketphone_5_Troubleshooting:
Pocketphone 5 Troubleshooting

Common problems with the Pocketphone 5 and how to fix them.

Phone Won't Turn On

A phone that shows nothing at all when the power button is held may have a dead battery or a fault on the board.

Dead battery

Plug the phone into a known-good charger for at least 30 minutes, then hold the power and volume-down buttons together for 15 seconds to force a restart.

Damaged charging port

Look into the port with a torch; lint packed into the port stops the plug from seating. Remove it gently with a wooden toothpick, never metal.

  • If the phone charges only at an angle, the port itself may be damaged and the board must be repaired.

Screen Flickers

Flickering after a drop usually means the display cable has come loose; reseat the display connector. If the flicker remains, replace the screen.

Phone Gets Hot While Charging

Some warmth is normal, but a phone too hot to hold, or a swollen case, means the battery is failing: stop using and charging it, and replace the battery.
pages.ifixit/How_to_Clean_a_Keyboard:
How to Clean a Keyboard

A sticky or crumb-filled keyboard can be cleaned at home without special tools.

Before you begin

Unplug the keyboard, or shut down the laptop and unplug its charger, before cleaning. Never pour liquid onto a laptop keyboard.

Instructions

Step 1

Turn the keyboard upside down and tap it gently.

Use compressed air at an angle to blow out crumbs.

Step 2

Dampen a lint-free cloth with isopropyl alcohol of 70 percent or more.

Wipe the tops of the keys. Do not let liquid drip between them.

Step 3

For a sticky key on a desktop keyboard, pull the keycap off with a keycap puller, clean under it with a cotton swab and alcohol, and press it back on.

Laptop keycaps break easily; check a guide for your model before removing one.

Warnings

Let the keyboard dry for at least an hour before plugging it back in. Water and alcohol left inside can short the circuits.

Ferries from the islands arrive at the old harbour every morning; buy tickets at the ferry office the day before.

The stone town is a maze of narrow lanes best explored on foot; cars cannot enter most of it.

pages.wikipedia/Mayflower_long:
Mayflower (long)

The Mayflower was an English ship that carried a group of English families, later called the Pilgrims, to North America in 1620.

Background

The Pilgrims were Separatists who had left the Church of England and lived for some years in Leiden in the Netherlands. They obtained a patent to settle in the north of the Virginia colony, and merchants in London paid for the voyage in return for a share of the profits. The Speedwell, a smaller ship, was to sail with the Mayflower but leaked and was left behind.

Voyage

The ship left Plymouth, England, on 16 September 1620 with 102 passengers and a crew of about thirty. Storms cracked one of its main beams, which the passengers helped to brace with a large iron screw. One passenger, John Howland, was washed overboard and pulled back by a rope.

Arrival

After 66 days at sea the ship sighted Cape Cod on 9 November. The master tried to sail south towards the Hudson River but turned back in dangerous shoals. The ship anchored off what is now Provincetown on 11 November 1620. The men signed the Mayflower Compact before going ashore, agreeing to make laws for the common good. Small parties explored the coast for several weeks in a shallop. They found corn buried by the Nauset people and took some of it. A party was attacked by Nauset men at a place they named First Encounter. In December the explorers found a harbour with fresh water and cleared fields. The settlers chose this site and named it Plymouth. The passengers stayed on board the ship through much of the winter while houses were built.

First winter

About half of the passengers and crew died in the first winter, of disease and cold. Only four of the eighteen married women survived.

Relations with the Wampanoag

In March 1621 Samoset, an Abenaki man who spoke some English, walked into the settlement. He brought Tisquantum, known as Squanto, who taught the settlers to plant corn and to fish. The Wampanoag leader Massasoit made a treaty of peace with the settlers that lasted for more than fifty years.

Later history

John Carver was chosen as the colony's first governor; after he died in April 1621, William Bradford took his place and led the colony for most of the next thirty years. The ship itself returned to England in April 1621 and was probably broken up around 1624.

pages.wikipedia/Earth:
Earth

Earth is the third planet from the Sun and the only astronomical object known to harbour life. About 71 percent of its surface is covered by water, mostly in the oceans.

Name

The modern English word Earth comes from Old English eorðe, meaning ground or soil. In Latin the planet is called Terra or Tellus.

Formation

Earth formed about 4.54 billion years ago from the disc of dust and gas around the young Sun. A collision with a body the size of Mars is thought to have thrown off the material that became the Moon. The surface cooled to form a solid crust within a few hundred million years. Water may have come from comets and from rocks that held it.

Structure

Earth's interior is divided into layers by their chemistry and their strength. The outer crust is thin, from about 5 kilometres under the oceans to 70 kilometres under mountains. Below it the mantle reaches down about 2,900 kilometres. The core is mostly iron and nickel, with a liquid outer part and a solid inner part. The inner core is about as hot as the surface of the Sun.

Plate tectonics

The crust and upper mantle are broken into plates that move a few centimetres a year. Where plates meet, earthquakes and volcanoes are common, including around the Pacific Ocean. Mountain ranges such as the Himalayas formed where plates collided. New ocean floor forms at ridges where plates move apart.

Surface

The land is shaped by water, wind and ice. The highest point is the summit of Mount Everest and the lowest on land is the shore of the Dead Sea. Deserts cover about a third of the land. Soils form slowly as rock breaks down and living things add organic matter.

Hydrosphere

The oceans hold about 97 percent of Earth's water. Most of the fresh water is frozen in ice sheets and glaciers. Sea water contains about 3.5 percent dissolved salts, mostly sodium chloride.

Atmosphere

The atmosphere is mostly nitrogen and oxygen. It shields the surface from most ultraviolet light and from small meteors. Weather happens in the lowest layer, the troposphere. The greenhouse effect keeps the average surface temperature at about 15 °C.

Magnetic field

Earth's magnetic field is made by currents in the liquid outer core. It turns away most of the charged particles of the solar wind. The magnetic poles wander and have reversed many times.

Orbit and rotation

Earth turns once on its axis in about 24 hours and goes round the Sun once in about 365.25 days. Its axis is tilted by about 23.4 degrees, which causes the seasons. The Moon's pull causes the tides.

Life

Life appeared on Earth at least 3.5 billion years ago. The biosphere includes all living things and the places they live. There have been five mass extinctions, including the one that ended the age of the dinosaurs.

Human geography

About eight billion people live on Earth. Most live in Asia, and more than half live in towns and cities. Humans have changed much of the land surface for farming and building.

About eight billion people live on Earth. Most live in Asia, and more than half live in towns and cities. Humans have changed much of the land surface for farming and building.

Climate zones

Climate varies with latitude, height and distance from the sea. The tropics are warm all year, while the poles are cold and dry. Monsoon winds bring heavy rain to South Asia each summer. Ocean currents carry heat from the equator towards the poles.

Biomes

Forests, grasslands, deserts and tundra each hold their own kinds of plants and animals. Tropical rainforests hold more than half of the known species of land animals. Coral reefs are among the richest places in the sea. Wetlands store water and slow floods.

People take fuels, metals and building stone from the crust. Fossil fuels formed over millions of years from buried plants and plankton. Fertile soil and fresh water are the resources most needed for farming. Many minerals are found in only a few countries, including some needed for batteries.

Earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, floods, droughts and tropical storms kill thousands of people in an average year. Tsunamis follow large undersea earthquakes and can cross whole oceans. Landslides are common on steep slopes after heavy rain. Early warning systems have reduced deaths from storms.

Exploration

Ancient Greek thinkers knew that Earth is round, and Eratosthenes estimated its size about 240 BC. Ships sailed round the world for the first time in the 1520s. Satellites have mapped the whole surface since the 1970s. The first photograph of the whole Earth from space was taken in 1967.

Moon

The Moon is Earth's only natural satellite and is about a quarter as wide. It always shows the same face to Earth. Its gravity slowly lengthens the day. The Moon's surface is covered in craters and dark plains of old lava.

Many cultures have seen Earth as a mother or a goddess. Pictures of Earth from space helped to start the modern environmental movement. The idea of a flat Earth was held by some ancient peoples but not by educated Europeans of the Middle Ages.

Human activity has raised the amount of carbon dioxide in the air and warmed the climate by more than one degree since 1850. Sea level is rising as ice melts and warm water expands. Forests are being cleared for farms, especially in the tropics. Pollution affects air, water and soil in many regions, including large cities.

In about a billion years the Sun will be bright enough to boil away the oceans. In about five billion years the Sun will swell into a red giant. Whether Earth will be swallowed is still debated.

Earth's diameter is about 12,742 kilometres. Its surface area is about 510 million square kilometres. It is the densest planet in the Solar System and the largest of the four rocky planets.

Pocketphone 3 Battery Replacement

Introduction

Use this guide to put a new battery into a Pocketphone 3 whose old one no longer holds a charge for a day.

Tools

  • Small cross screwdriver

  • Plastic opening pick

Parts

  • Pocketphone 3 battery

  1. Step 1

    • Run the battery down below a quarter before you start: a full battery can burn if it is pierced.

    • Switch the phone off.

    I used a guitar pick instead of the opening pick and it worked fine for the whole repair.

    Sam Tester - 3 March 2024

    How long did the old battery last for you before you changed it, and was it worth it?

    Kim Fixer - 3 March 2024

  2. Step 2

    • Remove the two small screws at the bottom edge, beside the charging port.

    Mine were stripped, a rubber band under the screwdriver helped me get them out in the end.

    Lee Hands - 3 March 2024

  3. Step 3

    • Warm the bottom edge of the screen for a minute.

    • Slide the opening pick under the screen and lift it gently; do not lift it more than ninety degrees.

  4. Step 4

    • Unplug the battery connector with the flat end of a plastic tool.

    • Pull the adhesive tabs under the battery slowly, keeping them flat.

    The second tab snapped on mine and I had to use a little isopropyl alcohol to free the battery.

    Ana Bench - 3 March 2024

  5. Step 5

    • Lay the new battery in place, plug in its connector and close the phone in the reverse order.

Riverton is the largest city of the river valley and the seat of its government, with a busy market and a university.

Understand

Riverton was founded as a ferry crossing and grew into a trading town; visitors who come in the dry season find it hot and dusty by noon. Riverton has a community of traders whose families came with the ferry. Most visitors stay in the old town of Riverton near the river, where the hotels and the market are. The tourist office in Riverton gives visitors a free map of the old town.

Get in

Riverton airport has daily flights from the capital, and visitors arriving by air can take a taxi into the centre in half an hour. Long-distance coaches stop at the north bus station of Riverton, a short ride from the old town. The train to Riverton runs twice a week from the coast and takes six hours.

Get around

By shared minibus

Shared minibuses run on fixed routes from the central square to every part of the city and cost a few coins a ride. They are crowded at rush hour; tell the driver your stop when you get on.

By taxi

Taxis wait at the hotels and the square; agree on the fare before you set off, or use the ride-hailing app that most drivers carry.

By motorbike taxi

Motorbike taxis are the quickest way through traffic jams, but ask for a helmet.

See

Visitors can learn about the ferry trade at the Riverton river museum, which is open every day except Monday. The old customs house of Riverton has a garden that visitors may walk around on their own. Visitors to Riverton should see the night market on Fridays.

Eat

Riverton is known for river fish grilled over charcoal, which visitors find at the stalls along the quay. Visitors who do not eat fish can try the bean stews of the old town.

Sleep

Riverton has hotels for every purse, and visitors in the high season should book ahead. The guest houses of Riverton near the station are cheap but noisy.

Stay safe

Riverton is calm by day, but visitors should keep to lit streets at night and watch their bags in the market.

Connect

There are many internet cafes around the market of Riverton for visitors who need to print or send a message.
pages.si/wiki_Oral_rehydration_therapy:
Oral rehydration therapy is a type of fluid replacement used to prevent and treat dehydration, especially from diarrhoea. It involves drinking clean water with small amounts of sugar and salts, chiefly sodium and potassium. Oral rehydration therapy can also be given through a tube in the nose. Use of oral rehydration therapy has been estimated to cut the risk of death from diarrhoea by most of it. Side effects may include vomiting and too much sodium or potassium in the blood. The recommended formulation includes sodium chloride, sodium citrate, potassium chloride and glucose. Glucose may be replaced by table sugar where it is not available. A number of other formulations are available, including versions that can be made at home. However, the use of homemade solutions has not been well studied. Oral rehydration therapy was first tried in the 1940s using electrolyte solutions with or without glucose, chiefly for mild patients, and came into common use only after it was found that glucose helps the gut take up sodium and water.

Medical uses

Oral rehydration therapy is used for children and adults with mild or moderate dehydration from any cause. Oral rehydration solution is taken in small sips, often from a spoon for a small child. Oral rehydration therapy is as good as fluids through a vein for most children, and costs far less. Oral rehydration solution should be given after every loose stool, together with the usual food.

History

Early trials of oral rehydration solutions were made in refugee camps, where fluids for the vein ran short. Oral rehydration therapy spread through village health workers in the 1970s and 1980s. Oral rehydration solution packets were made in many countries from the 1980s on.

Society and culture

Oral rehydration therapy has been called one of the great medical advances of its century. Oral rehydration solution is on lists of essential medicines.

Carbon dioxide

Carbon dioxide is a chemical compound with the chemical formula CO2. It is made up of molecules that each have one carbon atom covalently double bonded to two oxygen atoms. It is found in the gas state at room temperature, and as the source of available carbon in the carbon cycle, atmospheric CO2 is the primary carbon source for life on Earth. In the air, carbon dioxide is transparent to visible light but absorbs infrared radiation, acting as a greenhouse gas. Carbon dioxide is soluble in water and is found in groundwater, lakes, ice caps, and seawater. When carbon dioxide dissolves in water, it forms carbonate and mainly bicarbonate (HCO−3), which causes ocean acidification as atmospheric CO2 levels increase.

It is a trace gas in Earth's atmosphere at 421 parts per million (ppm), or about 0.04% (as of May 2022) having risen from pre-industrial levels of 280 ppm or about 0.025%. Burning fossil fuels is the primary cause of these increased CO2 concentrations and also the primary cause of climate change.

Its concentration in Earth's pre-industrial atmosphere since late in the Precambrian was regulated by organisms and geological phenomena. Plants, algae and cyanobacteria use energy from sunlight to synthesize carbohydrates from carbon dioxide and water in a process called photosynthesis, which produces oxygen as a waste product. In turn, oxygen is consumed and CO2 is released as waste by all aerobic organisms when they metabolize organic compounds to produce energy by respiration. CO2 is released from organic materials when they decay or combust, such as in forest fires. Since plants require CO2 for photosynthesis, and humans and animals depend on plants for food, CO2 is necessary for the survival of life on earth.

Carbon dioxide is 53% more dense than dry air, but is long lived and thoroughly mixes in the atmosphere. About half of excess CO2 emissions to the atmosphere are absorbed by land and ocean carbon sinks. These sinks can become saturated and are volatile, as decay and wildfires result in the CO2 being released back into the atmosphere. CO2 is eventually sequestered (stored for the long term) in rocks and organic deposits like coal, petroleum and natural gas. Sequestered CO2 is released into the atmosphere through burning fossil fuels or naturally by volcanoes, hot springs, geysers, and when carbonate rocks dissolve in water or react with acids.

CO2 is a versatile industrial material, used, for example, as an inert gas in welding and fire extinguishers, as a pressurizing gas in air guns and oil recovery, and as a supercritical fluid solvent in decaffeination and supercritical drying. It is a byproduct of fermentation of sugars in bread, beer and wine making, and is added to carbonated beverages like seltzer and beer for effervescence. It has a sharp and acidic odor and generates the taste of soda water in the mouth, but at normally encountered concentrations it is odorless.

pages.fx/Coral_bleaching:
Coral bleaching

Coral bleaching is the process when corals become white due to loss of symbiotic algae and photosynthetic pigments. This loss of pigment can be caused by various stressors, such as changes in temperature, light, or nutrients. Bleaching occurs when coral polyps expel the zooxanthellae (dinoflagellates that are commonly referred to as algae) that live inside their tissue, causing the coral to turn white. The zooxanthellae are photosynthetic, and as the water temperature rises, they begin to produce reactive oxygen species. This is toxic to the coral, so the coral expels the zooxanthellae. Since the zooxanthellae produce the majority of coral colouration, the coral tissue becomes transparent, revealing the coral skeleton made of calcium carbonate. Most bleached corals appear bright white, but some are blue, yellow, or pink due to pigment proteins in the coral.

Healthy coral
Bleached coral

The leading cause of coral bleaching is rising ocean temperatures due to climate change caused by anthropogenic activities. A temperature about 1 °C (or 2 °F) above average can cause bleaching.The ocean takes in a large portion of the carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions produced by human activity. Although this uptake helps regulate global warming, it is also changing the chemistry of the ocean in ways never seen before. Ocean acidification (OA) is the decline in seawater pH caused by absorption of anthropogenic carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. This decrease in seawater pH has a significant effect on marine ecosystems.

According to the United Nations Environment Programme, between 2014 and 2016, the longest recorded global bleaching events killed coral on an unprecedented scale. In 2016, bleaching of coral on the Great Barrier Reef killed 29 to 50 percent of the reef's coral. In 2017, the bleaching extended into the central region of the reef. The average interval between bleaching events has halved between 1980 and 2016. The world's most bleaching-tolerant corals can be found in the southern Persian/Arabian Gulf. Some of these corals bleach only when water temperatures exceed ~35 °C.

Bleached corals continue to live, but they are more vulnerable to disease and starvation. Zooxanthellae provide up to 90 percent of the coral's energy, so corals are deprived of nutrients when zooxanthellae are expelled. Some corals recover if conditions return to normal, and some corals can feed themselves. However, the majority of coral without zooxanthellae starve.

Normally, coral polyps live in an endosymbiotic relationship with zooxanthellae. This relationship is crucial for the health of the coral and the reef, which provide shelter for approximately 25% of all marine life. In this relationship, the coral provides the zooxanthellae with shelter. In return, the zooxanthellae provide compounds that give energy to the coral through photosynthesis. This relationship has allowed coral to survive for at least 210 million years in nutrient-poor environments. Coral bleaching is caused by the breakdown of this relationship.

pages.fx/Greenhouse_gas:
Greenhouse gas

Greenhouse gases (GHGs) are the gases in the atmosphere that raise the surface temperature of planets such as the Earth. What distinguishes them from other gases is that they absorb the wavelengths of radiation that a planet emits, resulting in the greenhouse effect. The Earth is warmed by sunlight, causing its surface to radiate heat, which is then mostly absorbed by greenhouse gases. Without greenhouse gases in the atmosphere, the average temperature of Earth's surface would be about −18 °C (0 °F), rather than the present average of 15 °C (59 °F).

This article is about the physical properties of greenhouse gases. For how human activities are adding to greenhouse gases, see Greenhouse gas emissions.

The five most abundant greenhouse gases in Earth's atmosphere, listed in decreasing order of average global mole fraction, are: water vapor, carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, ozone. Other greenhouse gases of concern include chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs and HCFCs), hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs), perfluorocarbons, SF
6, and NF
3. Water vapor causes about half of the greenhouse effect, but humans are not directly adding to its amount, so it is not a driver of climate change.

Carbon dioxide is causing about three-quarters of global warming and can take thousands of years to be fully absorbed by the carbon cycle. Methane causes most of the remaining warming and lasts in the atmosphere for an average of 12 years. Human activities since the beginning of the Industrial Revolution (around 1750) have increased carbon dioxide by over 50%, up to a level not seen in over 3 million years. The atmospheric methane concentrations have increased by over 150% during the same time period.

Without human influence, the natural flows of carbon between the atmosphere, terrestrial ecosystems, the ocean, and sediments would be fairly balanced. The vast majority of carbon dioxide emissions by humans come from the burning of fossil fuels. Further contributions come from agriculture and industry.: 687  Methane emissions originate from agriculture, fossil fuel production, waste, and other sources. If current emission rates continue then global warming will surpass 2.0 °C (3.6 °F) sometime between 2040 and 2070. This is a level which the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) says is "dangerous".

pages.fx/Methane_emissions:
Methane emissions

Increasing methane emissions are a major contributor to the rising concentration of greenhouse gases in Earth's atmosphere, and are responsible for up to one-third of near-term global heating. During 2019, about 60% (360 million tons) of methane released globally was from human activities, while natural sources contributed about 40% (230 million tons). Reducing methane emissions by capturing and utilizing the gas can produce simultaneous environmental and economic benefits.

Sources of methane emissions due to human activity (year 2020 estimates)

  Fossil Fuel Use (33%)
  Animal Agriculture (30%)
  Plant Agriculture (18%)
  Waste (15%)
  All Other (4%)

Since the Industrial Revolution, concentrations of methane in the atmosphere have more than doubled, and about 20 percent of the warming the planet has experienced can be attributed to the gas. About one-third (33%) of anthropogenic emissions are from gas release during the extraction and delivery of fossil fuels; mostly due to gas venting and gas leaks from both active fossil fuel infrastructure and orphan wells. Russia is the world's top methane emitter from oil and gas.

Animal agriculture is a similarly large source (30%); primarily because of enteric fermentation by ruminant livestock such as cattle and sheep. According to the Global Methane Assessment published in 2021, methane emissions from livestock (including cattle) are the largest sources of agricultural emissions worldwide A single cow can make up to 99 kg of methane gas per year. Ruminant livestock can produce 250 to 500 L of methane per day.

Human consumer waste flows, especially those passing through landfills and wastewater treatment, have grown to become a third major category (18%). Plant agriculture, including both food and biomass production, constitutes a fourth group (15%), with rice production being the largest single contributor.

The world's wetlands contribute about three-quarters (75%) of the enduring natural sources of methane. Seepages from near-surface hydrocarbon and clathrate hydrate deposits, volcanic releases, wildfires, and termite emissions account for much of the remainder. Contributions from the surviving wild populations of ruminant mammals are vastly overwhelmed by those of cattle, humans, and other livestock animals.

The Economist recommended setting methane emissions targets as a reduction in methane emissions would allow for more time to tackle the more challenging carbon emissions".

pages.fx/Ocean_acidification:
Ocean acidification

Ocean acidification is the ongoing decrease in the pH of the Earth's ocean. Over the past 200 years, the rapid increase in anthropogenic CO2 (carbon dioxide) production has led to an increase in the acidity of the Earth’s oceans. Between 1950 and 2020, the average pH of the ocean surface fell from approximately 8.15 to 8.05. Carbon dioxide emissions from human activities are the primary cause of ocean acidification, with atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO2) levels exceeding 410 ppm (in 2020). CO2 from the atmosphere is absorbed by the oceans. This chemical reaction produces carbonic acid (H2CO3) which dissociates into a bicarbonate ion (HCO−3) and a hydrogen ion (H+). The presence of free hydrogen ions (H+) lowers the pH of the ocean, increasing acidity (this does not mean that seawater is acidic yet; it is still alkaline, with a pH higher than 8). Marine calcifying organisms, such as mollusks and corals, are especially vulnerable because they rely on calcium carbonate to build shells and skeletons.

A change in pH by 0.1 represents a 26% increase in hydrogen ion concentration in the world's oceans (the pH scale is logarithmic, so a change of one in pH units is equivalent to a tenfold change in hydrogen ion concentration). Sea-surface pH and carbonate saturation states vary depending on ocean depth and location. Colder and higher latitude waters are capable of absorbing more CO2. This can cause acidity to rise, lowering the pH and carbonate saturation levels in these areas. There are several other factors that influence the atmosphere-ocean CO2 exchange, and thus local ocean acidification. These include ocean currents and upwelling zones, proximity to large continental rivers, sea ice coverage, and atmospheric exchange with nitrogen and sulfur from fossil fuel burning and agriculture.

A lower ocean pH has a range of potentially harmful effects for marine organisms. Scientists have observed for example reduced calcification, lowered immune responses, and reduced energy for basic functions such as reproduction. Ocean acidification can impact marine ecosystems that provide food and livelihoods for many people. About one billion people are wholly or partially dependent on the fishing, tourism, and coastal management services provided by coral reefs. Ongoing acidification of the oceans may therefore threaten food chains linked with the oceans.

The only solution that would address the root cause of ocean acidification is to reduce carbon dioxide emissions. This is one of the main objectives of climate change mitigation measures. Carbon dioxide removal from the atmosphere would also help to reverse ocean acidification. In addition, there are some specific ocean-based mitigation methods, for example ocean alkalinity enhancement and enhanced weathering. These strategies are under investigation, but generally have a low technology readiness level and many risks.

Ocean acidification has happened before in Earth's geologic history. The resulting ecological collapse in the oceans had long-lasting effects on the global carbon cycle and climate.
